sections.title: L Details about Metrics Calculation
sections.content: L.1 Command-level Scoring for Evaluating Models For each example, we extract the predicted command from the <output> tag and parse both the ground-truth and predicted commands into: <tool name>, <optional flags>, and <positional arguments> to know which flags take values and which flags are aliases. Tool score Tool_score is binary indicator: it is 1 if the predicted tool name exactly matches the ground-truth tool name, and 0 otherwise. Optional-argument F1. Ground-truth optional flags are grouped into alias sets (e.g., -h --help). predicted flag is counted as correct for group if it matches any alias in that group. Let be the number of ground-truth groups, Npred be the total number of predicted optional flags, and be the number of ground-truth groups that are hit by at least one predicted alias. We define 33 precisionopt = H/Npred and recallopt = H/G, and compute optional_f1 = 2 precisionopt recallopt precisionopt + recallopt . If both ground truth and prediction have no optional flags, we set optional_f1 to 1; if ground truth command has no optional flags while the predicted command has, we set it to 0. Positional-argument F1. The ground-truth and predicted positional arguments form 2 sets. We match each predicted argument to an identical ground-truth argument at most once: every successful match counts as true positive ; any remaining unmatched predicted arguments are false positives ; and any remaining unmatched ground-truth arguments are false negatives . We then define precisionpos = P/(T + ) and recallpos = P/(T + ), and compute positional_f1 = 2 precisionpos recallpos precisionpos + recallpos . If both lists are empty, we set positional_f1 to 1; if exactly one is empty, we set it to 0. Total score and Exact match Total score is the average of tool score, optional f1 and positional f1. And Exact match evaluates end-to-end command correctness which is 1 for generating correct canonicalized command, and 0 for any error in parameters. L.2 Dimensional Score Calculation To analyze model performance across functional security domains, we leverage Kalis metapackage taxonomy (Section 3) to assign each tool to one or more of = 23 capability dimensions. Each querycommand pair is therefore annotated with multi-hot vector v(i) {0, 1}D indicating the dimensions to which its ground-truth tool belongs. For each evaluation instance i, we project its scalar prediction score s(i) [0, 1] onto the corresponding capability dimensions by element-wise multiplication: s(i) = s(i) v(i). This assigns the score s(i) to all dimensions associated with the tool, while all other dimensions receive zero. Summing s(i) over all instances yields per-dimension performance scores for each model, enabling fine-grained analysis across the 23 cybersecurity capability dimensions. Example. Consider tool that is associated with three capability dimensions in Kalis taxonomy, corresponding to dimensions 2, 4, and 6 out of the total = 23. Its multi-hot encoding vector is therefore v(i) = (0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, . . . , 0) {0, 1}23, where the nonzero entries indicate the relevant capability dimensions and all remaining positions are zero. If the model assigns this instance scalar prediction score s(i) = 0.8, the projected dimensional score vector becomes s(i) = 0.8 v(i) = (0, 0.8, 0, 0.8, 0, 0.8, 0, . . . , 0). Thus, the same prediction score is assigned to each of the associated capability dimensions (2, 4, and 6), while having no effect on the others. Aggregating such vectors across all evaluation instances yields cumulative performance scores for each capability dimension.

sections.title: O Limitations
sections.content: KaliBench is designed as deterministic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating NLtoCLI function calling, and it inherits several limitations intrinsic to the CLI ecosystem and its documentation sources. Ground-truth commands are derived from Kali Linux tool manuals available at dataset construction time. As these manuals evolve across versions through the addition, deprecation, renaming, or reinterpretation of flags, some canonicalized commands may become outdated as upstream documentation changes. In practice, such effects are limited, as tools often maintain backward compatibility, and evaluation in the hinted setting is further insulated from drift by explicitly providing models with the tool documentation to follow. In addition, real-world tool documentation may occasionally contain inconsistencies or errors. For example, the regtree manual lists the -V option with conflicting semantics (-V, --no-values and 35 -V, --version), and several tools in the Impacket family document atypical short-option forms (e.g., -aesKey) that differ from common usage conventions (e.g., --aesKey). Such cases reflect the diversity and historical evolution of CLI interfaces rather than issues specific to KaliBench, and they make fully deterministic canonicalization inherently approximate when documentation diverges from observed behavior or when multiple variants coexist. Our LLM-as-Verifier pipeline substantially filters hallucinated flags and arguments by grounding validation in official manuals, but it remains imperfect; human verification of random subset indicates that residual errors are limited. Similarly, the alias-aware scoring mechanism relies on semi-automatically extracted alias groups and cannot capture all historical, distribution-specific, or community-adopted variants. Taken together, these considerations position KaliBench as controlled and well-defined abstraction of real-world CLI tool invocation. It is designed to support systematic, fine-grained evaluation of NL-to-CLI translation, while complementing execution-based or agentic evaluations in operational cybersecurity environments.
